name: Observability — per-tenant/per-route rolling rates, anomaly detection
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Application-metrics-niche observability / per-tenant + per-route SRE counters for alerting and decisioning
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A platform / SRE team computes per-tenant × per-route × per-method rolling RED metrics (RPS, error rate, latency p95/p99), per-tenant resource-use velocity, and anomaly windows, and exposes them in sub-ms reads to alerting, rate-limit, quota-enforcement and admission-control pipelines that need a decision in single-digit milliseconds.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power per-tenant noisy-neighbor detection: 'tenant X's RPS to POST /api/v2/search exceeded its 30-second rolling baseline by 5x — throttle now', with the decision served inline on the next request (token-bucket / leaky-bucket on top of beava counters). 2) Drive multi-window SLO burn-rate alerting (Google SRE 'fast 5m + slow 1h burn-rate' formulation) per (service, route, method, tenant_tier) without exploding Prometheus cardinality. 3) Feed an admission-control / quota-enforcement gate at the API gateway (Envoy ext_authz, Kong plugin, Cloudflare Worker) with sub-ms reads of (tenant_id, route, last-5m-error-rate, last-1m-p95-latency). 4) Compute per-tenant resource-use velocity (CPU-seconds, DB queries, LLM tokens, egress bytes) over rolling 1m/5m/1h windows for live cost-control and abuse detection, and surface 'top 10 tenants by velocity in last minute' for SRE triage. 5) Power per-route anomaly windows (z-score / EWMA against per-(tenant, route) baselines) that fire when current rate / latency / error-rate moves N sigma off, without standing up a separate ML pipeline.
domain_fit.event_shapes: request_completed {ts, tenant_id, route, method, status_code, latency_ms, bytes_in, bytes_out, region, pod_id, deployment_sha, user_id?, api_key_id?}, error_event {ts, tenant_id, route, method, error_class, error_code, status_code}, resource_usage {ts, tenant_id, route, cpu_ms, mem_bytes_peak, db_query_count, db_query_ms, llm_input_tokens, llm_output_tokens, cache_hits, cache_misses}, quota_consumed {ts, tenant_id, plan_tier, units, kind}, dependency_call_completed {ts, tenant_id, route, dependency, status, latency_ms}. Volume is dominated by request_completed (one per served HTTP/gRPC call) — typically equal to or higher than total user-traffic RPS. Key dimensions: tenant_id (or api_key_id / customer_id / workspace_id), route (templated path like /api/v2/projects/:id/items), method (HTTP verb or gRPC RPC name), status_code class (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx), region, plan_tier.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of count, rate (count over sliding window / window duration), velocity (rate-of-change of a rate), recency, distribution / percentile (t-digest / DDSketch / HDR-histogram), and ratio primitives. Per (tenant_id, route, method): count_5xx_1m, count_4xx_1m, rps_1m / rps_5m, error_rate_5m = count_5xx_1m / count_total_1m, latency_p50/p95/p99_1m (t-digest over the rolling window), bytes_out_velocity_5m. Per tenant_id: cpu_ms_sum_1m, db_query_ms_sum_1m, llm_tokens_sum_1m, n_unique_routes_1m, top-k routes by error_rate_5m (CMS / Top-K). For SLO burn-rate: requests_total_5m, errors_total_5m, requests_total_1h, errors_total_1h yielding 5m and 1h burn rates simultaneously (Google's multi-window formulation). For anomaly windows: EWMA + variance over per-(tenant, route) rate / latency / error-rate, exposed as 'current_z_score' features. distance / page-velocity-style primitives are also useful for time-since-last-error and time-between-bursts.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. Primary keys are tenant_id, (tenant_id, route), (tenant_id, route, method), (tenant_id, route, method, status_class), and (service, route, method) for non-tenant-aware SRE views. Secondary keys api_key_id, region, plan_tier, deployment_sha, pod_id (only for short-lived per-pod diagnostics). Per-user_id grain is generally outside this use case and lives in fraud / behavioral analytics; observability stops at the tenant or api-key level.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows are dominant for alerting (rolling 1m, 5m, 30m, 1h, 6h aligned with Google SRE multi-burn-rate windows). Tumbling 1m / 5m windows are used for the storage tier that gets rolled up to longer SLO compliance windows (24h, 7d, 28d, 30d). Session windows are not common here. Approximate aggregates are not only acceptable but mandatory at this cardinality: HLL for n_unique_user_id-per-tenant-per-minute, CMS + Top-K for 'hottest routes per tenant', t-digest / DDSketch / HDR-histogram for latency percentiles, EWMA / Welford's online variance for anomaly z-scores. Exact counts are needed only when the counter is the source-of-truth for usage-based billing (which is technically a sibling use case, not this one).
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is acceptable across the board for SRE alerting and admission-control: a slightly over-counted error rate fires a slightly earlier alert, which is the safe failure mode. Idempotency by (request_id) is desirable but optional. Strict exactly-once is required only when these same counters feed usage-based billing or a contractual SLA report — and the standard pattern is to fork the high-frequency observability stream from the lower-frequency billing stream at the source rather than ask beava to be exactly-once for both.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <5 ms for inline admission-control and rate-limit gates at the API gateway (single-digit-ms is the published target for Redis-backed rate limiters, and a gateway adding more than ~5 ms of overhead is rejected by most platform teams). Alerting / SLO burn-rate evaluation tolerates 100 ms — 1 s read latency. Dashboard refresh tolerates 1 — 5 s. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits comfortably inside the inline-gate budget — this is exactly the regime where Prometheus query latency (often 100 ms — 10 s for high-cardinality queries) disqualifies a generic TSDB.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second freshness is the differentiator vs Prometheus / Mimir, where the 15s — 60s scrape interval plus per-tenant rule-eval cadence puts the feature 30 — 120 s behind reality. For SLO burn-rate alerting, 1 — 30 s freshness is acceptable (the multi-window formulation explicitly trades freshness for false-alarm reduction). For per-tenant rate-limit / admission-control decisions, freshness must be <1 s — ideally <100 ms — because the decision is gating the very next request. beava's push-on-event model targets sub-second end-to-end and meets both regimes.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a mid-size SaaS observability footprint: 10k — 200k events/s (one event per served request, so EPS equals aggregate RPS of all instrumented services). Large platforms (Cloudflare-class edge, hyperscaler API gateways) land at 1M+ EPS aggregate. A single beava node at the published ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) covers a single mid-to-large platform; very large platforms must hand-shard by tenant prefix (which beava v0 does not provide in-process). Public reference points: Grafana Mimir benchmarks at ~360k samples/s on moderate hardware and scales to ~50M samples/s with a sizable cluster; VictoriaMetrics is comparable per-CPU-core. beava's value proposition here is not raw EPS — it's that the same EPS pre-aggregates into queryable per-entity feature rows at sub-ms read, which Mimir / VictoriaMetrics achieve only via recording rules with their own cardinality + freshness tradeoffs. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Write-dominant at the ingestion tier (one event per request, fan-out to multiple (tenant, route, method) keys), read-balanced at the alerting / decisioning tier (every API call into an inline admission gate is a beava read). The aggregate read:write ratio depends on whether inline gating is enabled: alert-only deployments are heavily write-skewed (~100:1 write:read), inline-gating deployments are closer to 1:1 because each request both writes its own event and reads features to decide on the next request.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by (tenant_id × route × method) cardinality. A typical mid-size SaaS has 1k — 100k tenants, 100 — 1k routes, 5 — 10 methods — so the keyspace is 1M — 10M composite keys. At ~500 B — 2 KB per key (a handful of sliding-window counters, a t-digest sketch of 100 — 500 B, EWMA state, recency timestamps), that is 0.5 — 20 GB hot state, well within a single modern node's RAM. Large platforms with 1M+ tenants tip into 100s of GB and require hand-sharding. The pathological case is including raw user_id or request_id in the key (which is what blows up Prometheus today) — observability deployments should explicitly NOT include those grains and instead push them to log / trace tiers. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: The classic 'cardinality explosion' shape Prometheus / Datadog struggle with: tenant_id (slowly-growing to explosive depending on plan tier — 1k — 1M+ tenants), route (bounded — typically <1k templated routes per service), method (bounded — single-digit), status_code class (bounded — 5 classes), region (bounded — single-digit-to-tens), deployment_sha (slowly-growing — one per deploy, days to weeks of relevance). The cartesian product is what drives the keyspace; the README's positioning of beava as 'cardinality survive' is exactly tuned to this product.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds to minutes for hot rate / latency counters (the rolling windows themselves are 1 m — 1 h, plus a small tail for late-arriving events). Hours to 30 days for SLO compliance counters (Google SRE recommends 28 — 30-day rolling SLOs, often kept as a small set of tumbling-day buckets that roll up). Per-deployment-sha state TTLs in days to weeks (relevance ends when the next deploy lands). For long-horizon reporting (>30 days), the deployment normally rolls beava counters up to a cold store (Mimir / Thanos / S3-Parquet) and discards the per-key hot state.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 1 — 5 features per inline admission-control / rate-limit decision (tenant_rps_1m, tenant_error_rate_5m, route_p95_latency_1m, plan_quota_remaining), batch_get one round-trip. 5 — 30 features per SLO burn-rate alerting cycle (per-(service, route) multi-window rates + budgets). 50 — 500+ features per dashboard refresh, which tolerates higher latency.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe — observability is derived state, not a regulated record. Losing 5 minutes of rolling counters during a node restart degrades alerting briefly (the windows refill) but does not produce a financial or auditable error. The SLO compliance counters that feed contractual SLAs are the exception and should be checkpointed to a durable backend at a low cadence; beava's WAL + snapshot story is sufficient for the hot window, with handoff to S3 / Parquet for the contractual report. The 'refuse-on-network-FS' restriction is fine — observability deployments universally co-locate state with the process anyway.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary regional and sidecar-next-to-API-gateway topologies — a beava instance per region next to the API gateway / load balancer / service mesh is the natural shape, with each region's counters local and a roll-up to a global tier (Mimir / Thanos / a beava aggregator) on the order of seconds-to-minutes. Multi-region active-active is rarely required because rate-limit / admission decisions are usually region-affinity-tolerant (a tenant's request lands in one region and is decided locally; global limits are reconciled asynchronously with eventual consistency, as in Envoy global ratelimit). The hard limit is that beava v0 has no in-process sharding, so very-large-fleet deployments (>684k EPS or >50 GB hot state per region) must hand-shard externally.

commercial_fit.who_buys: (a) Platform engineering / SRE teams at SaaS, fintech, AI/LLM, gaming and developer-tools companies who are hitting Datadog / New Relic / Dynatrace per-custom-metric cardinality bills and want to keep per-tenant granularity without paying per-time-series. (b) Multi-tenant SaaS platform teams who need per-tenant noisy-neighbor detection + admission control inline at the API gateway. (c) Edge / API-gateway teams (Envoy / Kong / Tyk / Cloudflare / Fastly users) who need a sub-ms rate-limit / quota counter that doesn't depend on Redis Lua, especially in distributions where the gateway and feature store can co-locate. (d) AI / LLM-platform teams who need per-tenant token-velocity counters for abuse / cost control on inference endpoints. The buyer in this domain is platform / SRE — explicitly NOT the application developer (who reads dashboards from Grafana / Datadog) and NOT the risk / fraud team.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Observability tools and platforms market is sized at $11.8B — $28.5B in 2025 by various analysts (Precedence Research, Research Nester, MarketsandMarkets), with multiple forecasts converging on $40 — $50B by 2030 — 2035 at 15 — 20% CAGR. Datadog's published custom-metrics-cardinality billing pressure is a public proxy for the cardinality-niche TAM: custom metrics regularly account for >50% of large Datadog bills, and large enterprises measure their custom-metrics-cardinality charge in millions of dollars per year (the 'Metrics Without Limits' product line and the existence of Chronosphere / Sawmills / Cribl / Bindplane / Edge Delta as standalone businesses validate the spend). beava's serviceable segment here is not the full observability TAM — it's the slice of platform/SRE teams who want per-tenant granularity inline for decisioning, which is materially smaller than the full observability market but still a 9-figure spend across the public-cloud + SaaS ecosystem. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Datadog / New Relic / Dynatrace custom-metrics-cardinality billing pressure — custom-metrics regularly account for >50% of a Datadog bill, with tenant_id / customer_id named as the dominant offender, and this is the explicit pain Chronosphere / Sawmills / Levitate were built to relieve. 2) Cardinality-induced query slowdowns in Prometheus / Mimir / Cortex (the GitHub Mimir issues #12602 / #7484 and discussions #2081 / #3292 all describe per-tenant ingestion-limit and series-limit failures in production). 3) AI / LLM platform cost control (per-tenant token velocity) — the GPU / token spend per tenant is now large enough that real-time visibility is a top-3 ask for any team running LLM endpoints. 4) Same-region in-process decisioning trend — service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, Envoy) and edge platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Fly Machines) all want a co-located feature store for inline gating rather than a round-trip to a remote Redis or Mimir. 5) Multi-window SLO burn-rate alerting (Google SRE workbook) has become the de-facto SRE pattern, and computing 5m + 1h burn rates per (service, route, tenant_tier) at scale is exactly the cardinality × freshness × read-latency combination Prometheus recording rules struggle with.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: SOC 2 is table-stakes (the observability backend handles request-level metadata that frequently includes PII via the user_id / api_key_id labels). GDPR / CCPA matter when user_id is one of the dimensions — beava's lack of TLS / auth in v0 is a blocker for any deployment outside a strictly trusted VPC, and the 'tombstone-by-user_id' primitive is required if user_id is ever an entity key. PCI-DSS scope creeps in when the observability backend ingests request paths containing card identifiers — best practice is to strip those upstream, which is an OTel-collector / API-gateway concern rather than a beava concern. Beyond that, this domain is not regulator-grade durability (unlike AML or billing).
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 1 — 3 days to a working 'per-(tenant, route, method) RPS + error_rate + p95 latency' demo on a laptop using @bv.event for request_completed and @bv.table for the rolling counters, fed by an Envoy access-log tail or an OTel-collector → HTTP-push shim. 1 — 2 weeks to a production pilot in front of an inline rate-limit / quota gate at the API gateway, gated mostly by adding TLS / auth (the v0 gap below) and by wiring up TTL / eviction policy for tenant_id cardinality.

competition.incumbents: Generic time-series + recording-rules stack: Prometheus + recording rules (the default OSS baseline), Grafana Mimir (multi-tenant Prometheus-compatible long-term storage with per-tenant limits and recording rules), Cortex (Mimir's predecessor), Thanos, VictoriaMetrics / VictoriaMetrics Cluster, M3DB, Wavefront, Netflix Atlas. High-cardinality-specialist observability backends: Honeycomb (columnar event store, high-cardinality-first), Chronosphere (control-plane-driven cardinality shaping over an M3 backend), Datadog (Metrics Without Limits two-tier pricing), New Relic, Dynatrace, Splunk Observability, Elastic Observability. ClickHouse-backed stacks: ClickStack / HyperDX, SigNoz, Uptrace, OpenObserve, Tinybird, Last9. Edge / per-tenant analytics: Cloudflare Workers Analytics Engine (unlimited-cardinality, SQL-queryable, equitable-sampling per index). Rate-limit / decisioning incumbents: Redis (Lua sliding-window-counter / token-bucket / leaky-bucket — the overwhelming default), Envoy global ratelimit (Lyft ratelimit service), Kong rate-limit plugin, AWS API Gateway throttling.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: For the per-tenant + per-route + sub-ms-read niche specifically: Redis (with Lua sliding-window-counter scripts) is the de-facto incumbent for inline gateway decisioning, and most production Envoy / Kong / Tyk deployments back their rate-limit plugin with Redis. Chronosphere Control Plane is the named competitor for cardinality-shaping inside the observability stack (per-team / per-service / per-tenant quotas, downsampling, label dropping). Honeycomb is the named competitor for high-cardinality query, but pushes queries through a columnar event store rather than a feature store — it answers 'show me p95 by (tenant, route) now' but does not serve a sub-ms read to an inline gate. Cloudflare Workers Analytics Engine is the closest architectural cousin (unlimited-cardinality, per-customer sampling, Workers-local) but is SQL-batch-queried, not feature-store-served. Levitate (Last9) and Sawmills are positioned as cardinality-aware observability backends. Most of these are not pure feature-servers — they bundle ingestion, storage, query, dashboards and alerting; beava sits underneath, as a pre-aggregation tier between event ingest and either an alerting evaluator or an inline gate.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack read latency vs Prometheus / Mimir query latency that runs 100 ms — 10 s on high-cardinality (tenant, route) recording rules — this is the inline-decisioning regime Prometheus is structurally not designed for. 2) Cardinality survive: the (tenant × route × method × status_class) keyspace is a per-entity feature row in beava, not a per-time-series in a TSDB, so the per-entity memory cost is bounded by the row count rather than blowing up the index. 3) 50+ aggregation primitives cover RED + Golden Signals + multi-window burn-rate + velocity + percentile (t-digest / DDSketch) features without writing PromQL recording rules or Lua-on-Redis. 4) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Mimir-cluster / Redis-cluster — fits a sidecar-next-to-API-gateway or per-region-hot-tier embedding model. 5) Apache-2.0, no open-core — attractive to platform teams who don't want to lock the cardinality tier into Chronosphere / Datadog / Honeycomb commercial terms. 6) Push-on-event over HTTP/JSON :8080 or framed TCP+msgpack :8081 maps directly to OTel-collector → HTTP-exporter or Envoy access-log-tail pipelines. 7) Velocity / recency primitives are first-class — beava can express 'rate-of-change of error_rate over last 30s' or 'time since last 5xx for this tenant' as feature reads, which Prometheus expresses as PromQL on every query (expensive) and Redis expresses as hand-rolled Lua.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 — disqualifying for any production deployment that ingests request-level metadata across trust boundaries (most of them); restricts beava today to in-VPC or behind-mTLS-proxy. 2) No in-process sharding — a single very large platform (>684k EPS or tens of GB hot state per region) must hand-shard externally, whereas Mimir / VictoriaMetrics Cluster / Datadog already shard internally. 3) No PromQL / SQL query surface — Prometheus, Mimir, ClickHouse, Honeycomb all let SREs write ad-hoc 'show me top 10 tenants by p95 latency in the last 10 minutes' queries; beava only serves the features it has been told to compute. This is a fundamental product gap for the 'replace my TSDB' framing and forces beava into the 'hot pre-aggregation tier in front of the TSDB' role. 4) No native multi-tenancy primitives (namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting on beava's own write path) — Mimir and Chronosphere have entire control-plane sub-products for this. 5) No long-term archive — losing 5 minutes of rolling counters on restart is fine for alerting, but contractual SLO reports need 28 — 30-day durable storage which still lives in Mimir / S3 / ClickHouse. 6) No triggers / 'fire when burn-rate crosses 14.4x' actions — alerting still has to poll, which is fine but is one round-trip slower than a callback. 7) No native PromQL recording-rule import — buyers migrating from Prometheus must rewrite their rules as @bv.table declarations, raising switching cost. 8) No documented OTel-collector exporter today — every other observability backend ships one. [uncertain]
competition.integration_surface: Producers: OpenTelemetry collector → HTTP exporter (the natural front door, but needs a beava-specific OTel exporter shim today), Envoy / Istio / Linkerd access-log tail → HTTP/TCP push, API gateways (Kong / Tyk / Apigee / AWS API Gateway via Lambda / Cloudflare Workers), service-mesh metrics adapters, Prometheus remote-write receiver compatibility (would be a strong adoption lever — does not exist in v0). Mobile / SDK direct push is not the path here; observability data is server-side. Consumers: inline admission-control / rate-limit gates (Envoy ext_authz, Kong custom plugin, Cloudflare Worker, Fastly Compute, in-house gateway), alert evaluators (Alertmanager, Grafana OnCall, PagerDuty Event Intelligence, in-house), dashboards (Grafana via a Beava data-source plugin — does not exist in v0 — or a thin proxy that translates PromQL-style range queries to beava get / batch_get).
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Mostly an external rules engine on the alerting side (Alertmanager, Grafana alerting rules, Datadog monitors, in-house Drools / OpenPolicyAgent / cedar gates for admission control) reading beava features via batch_get. Some buyers couple to an ML anomaly detector (Prophet / EWMA / isolation forest / a learned baseline) for adaptive thresholds — beava can serve the rolling-window features the detector needs, but the model itself lives outside beava. Pure feature-server role in both cases; beava is not the scoring engine.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava users on this use case identified. [uncertain] Comparable production references at incumbents: Cloudflare Workers Analytics Engine publishes its per-customer equitable-sampling architecture and is used inside Cloudflare for per-zone metrics; Chronosphere publishes ~84% data-reduction-on-average for customers migrating from Datadog / Prometheus; Honeycomb publishes high-cardinality SLO + anomaly-detection case studies; Grafana Mimir is publicly run by Grafana Cloud at billion-active-series scale with per-tenant limits; AWS publishes the Well-Architected SaaS Lens 'noisy neighbor' patterns; Lyft published the ratelimit service that became the Envoy global-ratelimit reference design (Redis-backed). The Datadog cardinality-cost-reduction narrative is a recurring topic in SRE blog posts (Sawmills, Cribl, Bindplane, Edge Delta, Last9 Levitate) and on r/sre / r/devops Reddit threads, validating the buyer pain even without a beava-specific reference.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads located on this topic. [uncertain] Broader community signal is strong: GitHub Mimir issues #12602 (ingester hitting series limits when scaling up), #7484 (limit per-series data points per minute), and discussions #2081 / #3292 / #4590 all describe the cardinality-explosion pain that beava's positioning addresses; Hacker News thread on the Grafana Mimir vs VictoriaMetrics performance comparison; SRE blog content on 'Why metric cardinality keeps exploding and how SRE leaders can stop it' (Sawmills, Chronosphere, Last9, OpenObserve, ControlTheory); Google SRE workbook chapter 'Alerting on SLOs' (multi-window multi-burn-rate) is widely cited.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated observability / per-tenant-RED demo identified in the repository. The python/beava/ directory contains no demos/ subtree at the time of review, and there is no examples/ directory at the repo root. A purpose-built demo (request_completed event → per-(tenant, route, method) rolling RPS / error_rate / p95-latency / SLO-burn-rate / EWMA-z-score, served via batch_get for an inline Envoy ext_authz gate) would be a natural addition and a strong differentiator vs. Prometheus + recording rules. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Low / passive at the SRE-observability core (the alerting counter is not under attack — services emit truthful access logs) but moderate at the inline-decisioning edge (tenants actively try to evade per-tenant rate limits, and the noisy-neighbor / abuse-control slice of this use case overlaps with the bot-defence and account-abuse use cases). The drift is from product changes (new routes, new tenants, new plan tiers, deploy-induced baseline shifts) rather than from an adversary trying to fool the counter; this is much less hostile than fraud (use cases 1a — 4) but more hostile than pure dashboards.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Replacing a full-stack observability backend (Prometheus / Mimir / Datadog / Honeycomb / ClickStack) — beava only serves features it has been told to compute, so it sits underneath the dashboard / ad-hoc-query tier rather than in place of it. 2) Logs and traces — beava is a metrics-shaped feature server; logs and distributed traces still belong in Loki / Elasticsearch / ClickHouse / Tempo / Jaeger. 3) Long historical lookback (>30 — 90 d) — beava is in-memory only; SLO compliance reports and incident retros still need a durable cold archive. 4) Cross-entity ad-hoc OLAP (joins across tenant × route × deploy_sha × pod) — that is ClickHouse / Druid / Pinot territory. 5) Source-of-truth for usage-based billing — exactly-once + 99.999% durability requirements push that into a sibling design (the same per-tenant counter can be computed twice, once in beava for sub-ms decisioning and once in a durable stream for billing). 6) Acting as the alerting evaluator UI — Alertmanager / Grafana / PagerDuty already own this surface; beava feeds it.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and an auth model (token / mTLS) on :8080, :8081 and :8090 — without these, beava cannot handle request-level metadata that frequently includes PII or routing secrets outside a strictly trusted VPC, which rules out any cross-team / cross-tenant production deployment. 2) Per-entity TTL / sliding-window eviction with a documented memory budget — tenant_id cardinality is the dominant operational risk and the buyer needs a 'set max RAM, evict-by-TTL-then-LRU' guarantee, especially for free-tier / trial-tenant explosions. 3) DDSketch / HDR-histogram / t-digest as documented first-class aggregations for latency p50/p95/p99/p999 (the README claims 50+ primitives but the latency-percentile story specifically must be airtight for SRE buyers, since averaging pre-computed percentiles is a textbook anti-pattern). 4) An OpenTelemetry-collector exporter (HTTP and TCP+msgpack variants) — every other observability backend ships one, and lack of one is a hard adoption blocker. 5) A Prometheus remote-write receiver — would let beava sit transparently behind existing Prometheus scrape configs and aggregate at the (tenant, route) grain without any application change; strongest adoption lever for the SRE buyer. 6) Multi-window burn-rate as a first-class primitive (compute 5m / 30m / 1h / 6h rates against a SLO target and expose a single 'burn_rate_max_over_windows' feature). 7) EWMA / Welford's online variance / streaming z-score primitives for anomaly windows, so 'current rate vs (tenant, route) baseline' is a feature read rather than a custom rollup. 8) Triggers / 'fire when feature crosses threshold' — necessary for alerting and admission-control without polling. 9) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant write-quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting on beava's own ingress for vendors embedding beava across many customer workspaces — this is exactly what Mimir's tenant-limits subsystem exists to do. 10) A Grafana data-source plugin (or a thin PromQL-subset proxy) so the same SLO dashboards that already exist on Prometheus can read beava features. 11) Optional long-term sink (Mimir remote-write, S3 / Parquet, ClickHouse) so the cold tier can live alongside without forcing the buyer to dual-write. 12) In-process or sidecar sharding by (tenant_id) prefix for very large platforms exceeding a single box.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly preferred. SLO burn-rate alerting and admission-control gates both want push-on-threshold semantics rather than poll-on-interval: 'fire when burn_rate_5m > 14.4x for 2m AND burn_rate_1h > 6x for 5m' (the Google SRE multi-window formulation) is naturally a trigger, and polling 100k (tenant, route) keys every 10 s to threshold them in an external evaluator is wasteful. Pure dashboard / range-query slices need only feature serving (the read is happening because something is about to render), not triggers.
